newsitem.title: USA: Cold weather blasts U.S. natgas to new 1996 highs.
newsitem.headline: Cold weather blasts U.S. natgas to new 1996 highs.

text.p: An unexpected cold front forecast for much of the U.S. later this week and next helped propel NYMEX spot natural gas futures to new highs Tuesday, and some gas analysts said the rally may not be over.

Bullish sentiment started to grip the futures market late last week, as intial forecasts for a few isolated pockets of cold this month evolved into expectations for a below-normal Arctic air mass destined to blanket much of the nation.

"Some of the longer-term forecasters are starting to change their tune," said Michael Barbis, analyst at UBS Securities in New York, referring to early winter outlooks calling for mostly seasonal temperatures.

Spot-December surged 32.8 cents, or 11 percent, Tuesday to close at $3.306 per million British thermal units, the highest level since December 21, 1995, when the spot contract soared to an all-time intraday high of $3.72.

While anything could happen before December goes off the board Thursday, particularly after the 25 percent gain seen in the last four sessions, few expected a sustained retreat until more moderate weather sets in.
"It's purely a weather play and the market could stay healthy for a while if we get cold," said Merrill Lynch analyst John Olson in Houston.
Rita Beale, analyst at Fimat Futures in Houston, also sees higher numbers ahead.
"I think we're still going higher this week. $3.50 is the next target (for December)," she said.

While stocks in key consuming regions like the Midwest and Northeast appear adequate, some said memories of last year still haunt operators, when inventories were drained to record low levels by a steady stream of cold air from Canada.

"There's plenty of supply to meet demand, but there's a lot of emotionalism over the cold," said Dick Sutton, principal at Houston-based consultants Jofree Corp, noting inventories in the east had now built up above 1995 levels.

But Beale said more than weather was driving the rally, and that despite comfortable levels back east, stocks nationwide were still well-below last year and likely to stay that way, ensuring minimal storage withdrawals early in the season.
"We started almost 200 billion cubic feet below last year, and people won't want to pull from storage in December, so they're willing to go into the cash and buy," she said.
Beale said the recent cold and forecasts for more through the month made significant stock declines likely in the next three American Gas Association (AGA) weekly storage reports.

Last week, AGA data showed total U.S. stocks at 85 percent of capacity, but still 170 bcf, or six percent, below last year. Eastern inventories, on the other hand, stood at 96 percent full and were slightly over 1995 levels.

But regardless of the broader fundamentals, with bidweek set to begin later this week, analysts said the cold-weather rally could not have come at a better time for producers who are likely to see December Gulf Coast indices well-above $3.00, up from November 1 prices in the $2.70 area.
